###### Abstract
Predicting the RNA and protein content of cells from routine H&E images could extend spatial molecular profiling to existing slide archives. However, both H&E–spatial proteomics and H&E–spatial transcriptomics paired datasets are limited by the number of available markers and the insufficient availability of high-quality, cell-resolved data.
In this paper, we introduce SCOPE, a unified framework for single-cell RNA and protein prediction from H&E images. At its core, SCOPE leverages the biological correspondence between genes and their encoded proteins to establish a shared molecular representation, enabling complementary supervision across transcriptomic and proteomic modalities. To extend prediction beyond directly supervised targets, we further introduce biologically informed biomarker co-encoding, which incorporates gene co-expression patterns, molecular interactions, and pathway relationships to transfer knowledge from observed to unseen markers.

We curated a dataset of 2.2 million paired tissue images and transcriptomic data across 32 organs to train OmiCLIP integrating histology and transcriptomics. Compared with 22 state-of-the-art models on 5 simulations, and 19 public and 4 in-house experimental datasets, Loki demonstrated consistent accuracy and robustness.
## Results
### Loki PredEx predicts ST gene expression from H&E images
Building on the success of Loki Align, Annotate and Decompose in analyzing tissue across the H&E image and transcriptomics data, we developed Loki PredEx to predict gene expression for image patches. # Body Map: How a Routine Tissue Image Reveals Genes ✎ express

Original: "A Multimodal Foundation Model of Spatial Transcriptomics and Histology for Biological Discovery and Clinical Prediction"

A microscope shows the shape of cells, and a new model adds a molecular portrait to it.

A pathologist stains a tissue section with hematoxylin and eosin — cells turn blue and pink, and under the microscope you can see their shape and arrangement. But which genes are active in each cell cannot be read from such an image. That requires a separate, expensive assay that reveals the activity of thousands of genes at once, but it is rarely performed.

The STORM model bridges these two worlds: it was trained on 1.2 million pairs of 'tissue image + gene activity map' from 18 organs.

STORM looks at a stained image and predicts which genes are turned on at each spot. It does so more accurately than other methods across 11 tumor types. The model works with different platforms (Visium, Xenium, Visium HD, CosMx) and requires no retuning. On data from 7245 patients across 23 independent cohorts, STORM predicted whether a patient would respond to immunotherapy and how the disease would progress better than standard biomarkers.

Such a tool turns a routine histological image into a molecular map. A doctor sees not only the shape of cells but also their internal program, and can choose treatment more precisely.

Hematoxylin stains cell nuclei blue, while eosin stains the cytoplasm pink. This dye duo has been used for over a hundred years and remains the mainstay in pathology.

As shown in Figure 1, we performed gene expression analysis of the TCGA breast cancer (TCGA-BRCA) cohort (n = 1082) to identify 200 groups of genes such that the expression of genes in the same group is maximally co-dependent. jina.title: What Does a Positive Stain Measure? From Fixed Tissue to Living Cell Biology: Lessons from the Stomach
jina.snippet:
## Introduction

A positive immunohistochemical stain can be among the most persuasive observations in experimental biology. It associates a molecular target with an identifiable cell, a subcellular compartment and an organised tissue. Nevertheless, the apparent precision of this localisation can conceal uncertainty about what has actually been measured. An antibody may detect a protein in a chemically fixed section without establishing its accessibility in a living cell. Membrane staining may identify a receptor without demonstrating its activation. Nuclear retention may indicate the presence of a repair protein without measuring its biochemical competence. These distinctions are familiar individually, but they are not always preserved when histochemical observations are translated into functional or clinical claims (Fritschy 2008; Shi et al. 2011).

This does not mean that immunohistochemistry (IHC) is inherently unreliable. Its value rests on the ability to associate molecular detection with tissue structure, often using assays whose analytical and clinical performance have been extensively validated. The difficulty arises when a conclusion extends beyond the property measured. Analytical validity, molecular localisation, functional inference and clinical utility are connected, but they are not interchangeable. A clinically useful threshold may be established through treatment-outcome evidence without representing a direct physical measurement of receptor activity or antibody access. Conversely, a technically reproducible signal may remain biologically ambiguous when its cellular origin, subcellular distribution or quantitative response is uncertain (Goldsmith et al. 2024).

jina.snippet:
## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12287294/)Abstract

Gene expression is an important process in which genes guide the synthesis of proteins, and molecular-level differences often lead to individual phenotypic variations. Combining molecular information at the nano-level with phenotypic information at the micron level can allow for the identification of a series of gene-level biomarkers related to image phenotypes and provide a more comprehensive way to understand the impact of genes on cell morphology. Currently, most studies in imaging genomics focus on tumors. However, tumor heterogeneity mitigates the reproducibility of gene-micro-correlations. Furthermore, research on the association between imaging features and gene expression patterns in multiple tissues is still lacking. This study aims to explore the correlations between the nuclear features of healthy tissue cells and RNA expression patterns. Based on 4306 samples of 13 organs from the largest human healthy tissue database, the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project, a deep learning-based automatic analysis framework was constructed to investigate the geno–micro–correlations across tissues. The proposed framework was used to quantitatively evaluate the nuclear morphological features of each healthy organ and identify gene sets specific to nuclear features in functionally similar organs. It revealed the biological significance of these gene sets through a pathway analysis, including cell growth, development, metabolism, and immunity. The results show that differences in nuclear morphological features of healthy organs are associated with differential RNA expression. By analyzing the correlation of differential patterns in multiple healthy organs, this study revealed the associations between gene expressions and phenotypes in multiple organs.

jina.snippet:
## Abstract

The tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) encompasses many heterogeneous cell types that engage in extensive crosstalk among the cancer, immune, and stromal components. The spatial organization of these different cell types in TIME could be used as biomarkers for predicting drug responses, prognosis and metastasis. Recently, deep learning approaches have been widely used for digital histopathology images for cancer diagnoses and prognoses. Furthermore, some recent approaches have attempted to integrate spatial and molecular omics data to better characterize the TIME. In this review we focus on machine learning-based digital histopathology image analysis methods for characterizing tumor ecosystem. In this review, we will consider three different scales of histopathological analyses that machine learning can operate within: whole slide image (WSI)-level, region of interest (ROI)-level, and cell-level. We will systematically review the various machine learning methods in these three scales with a focus on cell-level analysis. We will provide a perspective of workflow on generating cell-level training data sets using immunohistochemistry markers to “weakly-label” the cell types. We will describe some common steps in the workflow of preparing the data, as well as some limitations of this approach. Finally, we will discuss future opportunities of integrating molecular omics data with digital histopathology images for characterizing tumor ecosystem.

jina.title: How to Read Your Breast Cancer Pathology Report
jina.snippet:
The pathology report describes important characteristics of the breast cancer. This information helps you and your doctors choose the best treatments for you and your unique situation.

The term “pathology report” makes it sound like you’ll get just one report with all the information in it. But that’s not what happens. There’s more than one type of pathology report.

You’ll receive a report of results each time a test is done. Because not all labs do all tests, you’ll likely receive several different reports.

Together, all these reports make up your pathology report. It’s a good idea to keep all the reports in one place so when you visit your doctors you can discuss any of the results.

Pathologists are doctors who specialize in making a diagnosis by looking at tissue and cells, usually with the help of a microscope. By examining breast tissue and cells, a breast pathologist will issue a report — the pathology report — that describes the diagnosis. At this point you may receive a diagnosis of breast cancer. The pathologist may then do more tests on a sample of your blood or cancer tissue removed from your body to further describe the specific type of breast cancer.

There are two main types of pathology reports:

*   a biopsy pathology report

*   an excision pathology report with a synoptic summary

The biopsy pathology report describes what is found in the small sample of tissue removed during the [biopsy](https://www.breastcancer.org/screening-testing/breast-biopsy). If the biopsy pathology report finds breast cancer, in most cases you will have surgery to remove the entire cancer, which doctors call an excision.

The synoptic summary in an excision pathology report describes all the characteristics of the whole cancer.

keenable.title: Predicting Single-Cell Spatial Gene Expression from H&E using Pathology Foundation Models
keenable.snippet: Predicting gene expression directly from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images offers a scalable and cost-effective approach to deriving spatial molecular insights from routine histology. Pathology foundation models, typically pretrained using tile-level objectives, may not adequately capture the fine-grained cellular features required for single-cell molecular prediction. In this work, we systematically evaluate and establish domain-informed and task-specific strategies for adapting pathology foundation models to single-cell spatial gene expression prediction. Using paired H&E and Xenium 5K data, our approach improves mean gene-wise Pearson correlation by 2.67× over the standard zero-shot baseline and achieves state-of-the-art performance on this task. We demonstrate strong gene-detection performance across the full gene panel (AUROC = 0.800) and importantly identify that predictive performance varies substantially across biological contexts, with our model achieving its highest Pearson correlation for spatially variable genes (r = 0.643). Our findings demonstrate that, despite the challenges of sparse single-cell measurements, H&E-derived representations can recover biologically meaningful spatial expression patterns, highlighting both the opportunities and limitations of morphology-based molecular inference at cellular resolution.

keenable.title: Towards Scalable Context-Aware Single-Cell Spatial Transcriptomics Prediction from Histology Images
keenable.snippet:
Predicting gene expression from H&E-stained histology images offers a scalable alternative to costly spatial transcriptomics, yet most existing methods operate at the spot level, where signals from multiple cells are aggregated and critical cellular heterogeneity is obscured. Extending this paradigm to single-cell resolution is non-trivial. Naively applying pathology foundation models faces a scale mismatch: their patch-level representations mix multiple cells, whereas per-cell cropping or resizing distorts morphology and removes local context. Conversely, segmentation-based models without strong pretrained visual encoders often lack the morphological representation capacity needed for accurate molecular prediction and inherit errors from imperfect cell boundary masks. Here, we present CELLO, an efficient end-to-end framework that performs a single pathology foundation model forward pass per image and uses grid sampling to extract location-specific features for all cells simultaneously. We further introduce a distance-decay cross-attention module that refines each cell representation using spatially biased local morphological context. Using 52 public Xenium–H&E pairs from HEST-1k that span 12 organs and approximately 10 million cells, CELLO improves the average predictive accuracy over the evaluated baselines while reducing the mean whole-slide inference time compared to DeepSpot2Cell, a 14.0× speed-up on average that excludes upstream cell segmentation. Our work establishes a scalable foundation for single-cell gene expression prediction from H&E images. Code is available at https://github.com/zjgao02/CELLO.

To democratize spatial molecular profiling, numerous computational methods have been developed to directly infer ST profiles from ubiquitous H&E images He et al. (2020); Xie et al. keenable.title: SCOPE: Single-Cell Omics Prediction from Histology via RNA–Protein Prior Enhancement
keenable.snippet: Predicting the RNA and protein content of cells from routine H&E images could extend spatial molecular profiling to existing slide archives. However, both H&E–spatial proteomics and H&E–spatial transcriptomics paired datasets are limited by the number of available markers and the insufficient availability of high-quality, cell-resolved data. We present SCOPE (Single-Cell Omics Prediction via RNA–protein prior Enhancement), a unified framework that leverages biologically complementary information between RNA and proteins to address the limited availability of single-omics supervision. Our key insight is that, although RNA and proteins represent distinct molecular modalities, their biological relationships provide valuable shared knowledge that can benefit single-omics prediction tasks. To this end, SCOPE introduces biologically informed biomarker priors to enhance shared gene-level representations, enabling knowledge transfer across RNA and protein modalities through gene–protein correspondence and molecular associations. By exploiting these complementary relationships, SCOPE enables both prediction tasks to benefit from a shared backbone enriched with cross-omics biological knowledge. Furthermore, its biomarker correlation design facilitates the prediction of unseen markers, extending spatially resolved molecular profiling beyond directly supervised targets. Across test datasets spanning 16 organs, SCOPE improves the average RNA Pearson correlation over the strongest baseline by 8.8%. On two external protein cohorts, it improves the average Pearson correlation over the strongest baseline by 9.7% for seen markers and 11.9% for unseen markers.

keenable.title: From WSIs to Bulk, Spatial and Single-Cell Transcriptomics via Multi-Scale Graph Neural Networks
keenable.snippet:
Understanding the spatial distribution of gene expression is key to studying complex diseases like cancer. While Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) and Single-Cell Transcriptomics (scT) provide high-resolution insights, they remain expensive and scarce. In contrast, standard histopathology Whole-Slide Images (WSIs) paired with bulk RNA sequencing are widely available. This work introduces a Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network (GNN) capable of simultaneously predicting bulk, spatial, and single-cell transcriptomics directly from WSIs. By extracting morphological features using a Pathology Foundation Model (PFM) (UNI2-h) and constructing spatial graphs at both patch and cell levels, the model learns the hierarchical relationships within the tissue. The network is trained on a combined dataset of The Cancer Genome Atlas Program (TCGA), Visium, and Xenium samples across lung, kidney, and breast tissues. A hybrid training strategy is employed, leveraging direct supervision alongside weakly supervised consistency losses to ensure predictions align across biological scales. Results show the model accurately predicts gene expression at the slide level and moderately at the patch level (strongest on Xenium), and achieves moderate correlation at the challenging single-cell level. Furthermore, downstream tasks explore the clinical relevance of these predictions, demonstrating their utility in survival analysis, spatial hazard mapping, and tumor classification via molecular signatures.

On the other hand, histopathology is already a common practice in cancer diagnosis, producing hematoxylin and eosin-stained WSIs. WSIs are high-resolution digital representations of histopathology slides that capture the complete morphological context of the tissue. They preserve cellular structures, tissue architecture and spatial organization of cells.

keenable.title: SpaFactor: Lightweight Spatial Context-Aware Gene Program Modeling for Histology-to-Transcriptomics Inference
keenable.snippet: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) profiles gene expression within tissue architecture, but its cost and experimental complexity limit routine use. Predicting spatial expression from routinely available hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images therefore offers a scalable alternative. However, conventional methods often fit high-dimensional gene outputs as independent targets, overlooking the biological coordination among genes while remaining vulnerable to high-dimensional noise and overfitting. Existing attempts to address this limitation often rely on computationally heavy graph networks or complex auxiliary supervision. We therefore introduce SpaFactor, a lightweight and efficient low-rank morphology–program–gene factorization framework. At the input, SpaFactor efficiently fuses the visual representation of the central spot with multiscale local and regional neighborhood context, yielding a histologic representation that captures cellular morphology and microenvironmental heterogeneity. For modeling, a residual MLP stably learns a nonlinear mapping from the tissue microenvironment to low-dimensional latent gene programs. These activities are decoded through shared gene loadings into coordinated multi-gene expression predictions. Across five public cohorts, SpaFactor achieves the best aggregate performance, with particularly clear improvements for spatially variable genes, and more faithfully recovers biologically organized spatial patterns. These results demonstrate that lightweight joint modeling of tissue context and gene programs can improve both predictive accuracy and biological fidelity.

keenable.title: CytoFormer: A Molecularly Supervised Cell Foundation Model for Histopathology Cell Classification
keenable.snippet: Identifying cell types directly from routine haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) histology would enable single-cell analysis at scale, but training such models has relied on manual pathologist annotations, which are slow, expensive and unreliable for many cell types. We instead supervise morphology with molecules. Imaging-based spatial transcriptomics profiles individual cells in situ on a section that can afterwards be stained with H&E, so that molecular identity and morphology are observed for the same physical cell. We assembled 81 such paired Xenium sections spanning 16 organs, derived per-cell labels by clustering, marker-gene annotation, organ-wise human review and quality control, and mapped them onto the cell types commonly reported in each organ. This yielded 15.4 million cells, each with a paired H&E image patch and one of 23 cell types, on which we trained CytoFormer, a cell foundation model with a multi-task, per-organ classification head. On spatially held-out tissue CytoFormer reached an accuracy of 0.85 and a macro-F1 of 0.78 across all 16 organs, and its predictions reproduced the tissue architecture of an entire held-out section. The representation also transfers: with the encoder frozen, a linear head on CytoFormer features performed better than six pathology foundation models on four expert-annotated benchmarks, including on organs and cell types that were not part of pretraining. Finally, in an interactive active-learning setting, CytoFormer's embeddings are markedly more label-efficient than existing pathology foundation models, detecting normal epithelium amid look-alike tumour with an F1 of 0.82 from only a few annotations and leading the strongest baseline by 0.13 in F1. CytoFormer turns paired H&E and spatial transcriptomics into a reusable, label-efficient representation for cell-level analysis of routine histology.

keenable.title: AI Predicts Cellular RNA and Proteins From Routine Hospital Slides
keenable.snippet:
A new artificial intelligence framework successfully reconstructs thousands of hidden cellular molecular profiles directly from routine hospital microscope slides. By analyzing standard tissue sections stained with the pink and purple dyes common in pathology labs, the model predicts both RNA transcript activity and protein distributions at single-cell resolution. Researchers developed the system to unlock molecular insights from massive archives of historical patient samples without requiring expensive, specialized spatial assays.
## Bridging RNA and Protein Data Across Unpaired Tissues
Obtaining detailed maps of gene expression and protein markers across a tissue sample usually demands technically demanding techniques like in situ spatial transcriptomics or multiplex immunofluorescence. Because these advanced assays are costly, laboratories rarely perform both RNA and protein measurements on the exact same tissue section. The research team behind the new model, [published on the arXiv preprint server](http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24104v1), sought to overcome this hurdle by creating a unified system called SCOPE, which stands for Single-Cell Omics Prediction via RNA-protein prior Enhancement.
Led by computer scientists and bioinformaticians from Harvard Medical School, Stanford University, and the Beijing University of Civil Engineering and Architecture, the authors designed their approach around biological connections. Although RNA molecules and proteins represent distinct molecular types, the genes that encode them share a natural biological link. The framework exploits this correspondence to allow supervision from either RNA data or protein data to strengthen a shared gene-level representation.

keenable-realtime.title: SpaFactor: Lightweight Spatial Context-Aware Gene Program Modeling for Histology-to-Transcriptomics Inference
keenable-realtime.snippet: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) profiles gene expression within tissue architecture, but its cost and experimental complexity limit routine use. Predicting spatial expression from routinely available hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images therefore offers a scalable alternative. However, conventional methods often fit high-dimensional gene outputs as independent targets, overlooking the biological coordination among genes while remaining vulnerable to high-dimensional noise and overfitting. Existing attempts to address this limitation often rely on computationally heavy graph networks or complex auxiliary supervision. We therefore introduce SpaFactor, a lightweight and efficient low-rank morphology–program–gene factorization framework. At the input, SpaFactor efficiently fuses the visual representation of the central spot with multiscale local and regional neighborhood context, yielding a histologic representation that captures cellular morphology and microenvironmental heterogeneity. For modeling, a residual MLP stably learns a nonlinear mapping from the tissue microenvironment to low-dimensional latent gene programs. These activities are decoded through shared gene loadings into coordinated multi-gene expression predictions. Across five public cohorts, SpaFactor achieves the best aggregate performance, with particularly clear improvements for spatially variable genes, and more faithfully recovers biologically organized spatial patterns. These results demonstrate that lightweight joint modeling of tissue context and gene programs can improve both predictive accuracy and biological fidelity.

keenable-realtime.title: CytoFormer: A Molecularly Supervised Cell Foundation Model for Histopathology Cell Classification
keenable-realtime.snippet: Identifying cell types directly from routine haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) histology would enable single-cell analysis at scale, but training such models has relied on manual pathologist annotations, which are slow, expensive and unreliable for many cell types. We instead supervise morphology with molecules. Imaging-based spatial transcriptomics profiles individual cells in situ on a section that can afterwards be stained with H&E, so that molecular identity and morphology are observed for the same physical cell. We assembled 81 such paired Xenium sections spanning 16 organs, derived per-cell labels by clustering, marker-gene annotation, organ-wise human review and quality control, and mapped them onto the cell types commonly reported in each organ. This yielded 15.4 million cells, each with a paired H&E image patch and one of 23 cell types, on which we trained CytoFormer, a cell foundation model with a multi-task, per-organ classification head. On spatially held-out tissue CytoFormer reached an accuracy of 0.85 and a macro-F1 of 0.78 across all 16 organs, and its predictions reproduced the tissue architecture of an entire held-out section. The representation also transfers: with the encoder frozen, a linear head on CytoFormer features performed better than six pathology foundation models on four expert-annotated benchmarks, including on organs and cell types that were not part of pretraining. Finally, in an interactive active-learning setting, CytoFormer's embeddings are markedly more label-efficient than existing pathology foundation models, detecting normal epithelium amid look-alike tumour with an F1 of 0.82 from only a few annotations and leading the strongest baseline by 0.13 in F1. CytoFormer turns paired H&E and spatial transcriptomics into a reusable, label-efficient representation for cell-level analysis of routine histology.

Abstract

We demonstrate strong gene-detection performance across the full gene panel (AUROC = 0.800) and importantly identify that predictive performance varies substantially across biological contexts, with our model achieving its highest Pearson correlation for spatially variable genes (r = 0.643). Our findings demonstrate that, despite the challenges of sparse single-cell measurements, H&E-derived representations can recover biologically meaningful spatial expression patterns, highlighting both the opportunities and limitations of morphology-based molecular inference at cellular resolution.

Machine learning unlocks hidden patterns
For the study, researchers applied machine learning techniques to analyze tissue images taken from healthy human donors, which enabled them to unlock hidden signs of aging and gene activity that appear in human cells. Cell appearance is tied to both genes and the aging processes.

One of the machine learning models, they said, can predict gene expression based on an image, with some tissue samples—lung, heart, and testis—showing particularly strong predictive accuracy.

Overall, researchers found that the shape, size, and structure of cell nuclei carry a lot of biological information. They found 906 points in the human genome that were strongly tied to nuclei appearance in different tissues. There were also strong connections between nuclear shape and gene activity.

seltz.snippet:
## Abstract

Defining the protein profiles of tissues and organs is critical to understanding the unique characteristics of the various cell types in the human body. In this study, we report on an anatomically comprehensive analysis of 4842 protein profiles in 48 human tissues and 45 human cell lines. A detailed analysis of over 2 million manually annotated, high‐resolution, immunohistochemistry‐based images showed a high fraction (>65%) of expressed proteins in most cells and tissues, with very few proteins (<2%) detected in any single cell type. This study suggests that tissue specificity is achieved by precise regulation of protein levels in space and time, and that different tissues in the body acquire their unique characteristics by controlling not which proteins are expressed but how much of each is produced.

ultimate.title: Predicting Single-Cell Spatial Gene Expression from H&E using Pathology Foundation Models
ultimate.snippet: Predicting gene expression directly from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images offers a scalable and cost-effective approach to deriving spatial molecular insights from routine histology. Pathology foundation models, typically pretrained using tile-level objectives, may not adequately capture the fine-grained cellular features required for single-cell molecular prediction. In this work, we systematically evaluate and establish domain-informed and task-specific strategies for adapting pathology foundation models to single-cell spatial gene expression prediction. Using paired H&E and Xenium 5K data, our approach improves mean gene-wise Pearson correlation by 2.67× over the standard zero-shot baseline and achieves state-of-the-art performance on this task. We demonstrate strong gene-detection performance across the full gene panel (AUROC = 0.800) and importantly identify that predictive performance varies substantially across biological contexts, with our model achieving its highest Pearson correlation for spatially variable genes (r = 0.643). Our findings demonstrate that, despite the challenges of sparse single-cell measurements, H&E-derived representations can recover biologically meaningful spatial expression patterns, highlighting both the opportunities and limitations of morphology-based molecular inference at cellular resolution.

ultimate.title: Towards Scalable Context-Aware Single-Cell Spatial Transcriptomics Prediction from Histology Images
ultimate.snippet:
Predicting gene expression from H&E-stained histology images offers a scalable alternative to costly spatial transcriptomics, yet most existing methods operate at the spot level, where signals from multiple cells are aggregated and critical cellular heterogeneity is obscured. Extending this paradigm to single-cell resolution is non-trivial. Naively applying pathology foundation models faces a scale mismatch: their patch-level representations mix multiple cells, whereas per-cell cropping or resizing distorts morphology and removes local context. Conversely, segmentation-based models without strong pretrained visual encoders often lack the morphological representation capacity needed for accurate molecular prediction and inherit errors from imperfect cell boundary masks. Here, we present CELLO, an efficient end-to-end framework that performs a single pathology foundation model forward pass per image and uses grid sampling to extract location-specific features for all cells simultaneously. We further introduce a distance-decay cross-attention module that refines each cell representation using spatially biased local morphological context. Using 52 public Xenium–H&E pairs from HEST-1k that span 12 organs and approximately 10 million cells, CELLO improves the average predictive accuracy over the evaluated baselines while reducing the mean whole-slide inference time compared to DeepSpot2Cell, a 14.0× speed-up on average that excludes upstream cell segmentation. Our work establishes a scalable foundation for single-cell gene expression prediction from H&E images. Code is available at https://github.com/zjgao02/CELLO.

ultimate.title: SCOPE: Single-Cell Omics Prediction from Histology via RNA–Protein Prior Enhancement
ultimate.snippet: Predicting the RNA and protein content of cells from routine H&E images could extend spatial molecular profiling to existing slide archives. However, both H&E–spatial proteomics and H&E–spatial transcriptomics paired datasets are limited by the number of available markers and the insufficient availability of high-quality, cell-resolved data. We present SCOPE (Single-Cell Omics Prediction via RNA–protein prior Enhancement), a unified framework that leverages biologically complementary information between RNA and proteins to address the limited availability of single-omics supervision. Our key insight is that, although RNA and proteins represent distinct molecular modalities, their biological relationships provide valuable shared knowledge that can benefit single-omics prediction tasks. To this end, SCOPE introduces biologically informed biomarker priors to enhance shared gene-level representations, enabling knowledge transfer across RNA and protein modalities through gene–protein correspondence and molecular associations. By exploiting these complementary relationships, SCOPE enables both prediction tasks to benefit from a shared backbone enriched with cross-omics biological knowledge. Furthermore, its biomarker correlation design facilitates the prediction of unseen markers, extending spatially resolved molecular profiling beyond directly supervised targets. Across test datasets spanning 16 organs, SCOPE improves the average RNA Pearson correlation over the strongest baseline by 8.8%. On two external protein cohorts, it improves the average Pearson correlation over the strongest baseline by 9.7% for seen markers and 11.9% for unseen markers.

ultimate.title: From WSIs to Bulk, Spatial and Single-Cell Transcriptomics via Multi-Scale Graph Neural Networks
ultimate.snippet:
Understanding the spatial distribution of gene expression is key to studying complex diseases like cancer. While Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) and Single-Cell Transcriptomics (scT) provide high-resolution insights, they remain expensive and scarce. In contrast, standard histopathology Whole-Slide Images (WSIs) paired with bulk RNA sequencing are widely available. This work introduces a Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network (GNN) capable of simultaneously predicting bulk, spatial, and single-cell transcriptomics directly from WSIs. By extracting morphological features using a Pathology Foundation Model (PFM) (UNI2-h) and constructing spatial graphs at both patch and cell levels, the model learns the hierarchical relationships within the tissue. The network is trained on a combined dataset of The Cancer Genome Atlas Program (TCGA), Visium, and Xenium samples across lung, kidney, and breast tissues. A hybrid training strategy is employed, leveraging direct supervision alongside weakly supervised consistency losses to ensure predictions align across biological scales. Results show the model accurately predicts gene expression at the slide level and moderately at the patch level (strongest on Xenium), and achieves moderate correlation at the challenging single-cell level. Furthermore, downstream tasks explore the clinical relevance of these predictions, demonstrating their utility in survival analysis, spatial hazard mapping, and tumor classification via molecular signatures.

On the other hand, histopathology is already a common practice in cancer diagnosis, producing hematoxylin and eosin-stained WSIs. WSIs are high-resolution digital representations of histopathology slides that capture the complete morphological context of the tissue. They preserve cellular structures, tissue architecture and spatial organization of cells.

ultimate.title: SpaFactor: Lightweight Spatial Context-Aware Gene Program Modeling for Histology-to-Transcriptomics Inference
ultimate.snippet: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) profiles gene expression within tissue architecture, but its cost and experimental complexity limit routine use. Predicting spatial expression from routinely available hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images therefore offers a scalable alternative. However, conventional methods often fit high-dimensional gene outputs as independent targets, overlooking the biological coordination among genes while remaining vulnerable to high-dimensional noise and overfitting. Existing attempts to address this limitation often rely on computationally heavy graph networks or complex auxiliary supervision. We therefore introduce SpaFactor, a lightweight and efficient low-rank morphology–program–gene factorization framework. At the input, SpaFactor efficiently fuses the visual representation of the central spot with multiscale local and regional neighborhood context, yielding a histologic representation that captures cellular morphology and microenvironmental heterogeneity. For modeling, a residual MLP stably learns a nonlinear mapping from the tissue microenvironment to low-dimensional latent gene programs. These activities are decoded through shared gene loadings into coordinated multi-gene expression predictions. Across five public cohorts, SpaFactor achieves the best aggregate performance, with particularly clear improvements for spatially variable genes, and more faithfully recovers biologically organized spatial patterns. These results demonstrate that lightweight joint modeling of tissue context and gene programs can improve both predictive accuracy and biological fidelity.

ultimate.title: CytoFormer: A Molecularly Supervised Cell Foundation Model for Histopathology Cell Classification
ultimate.snippet: Identifying cell types directly from routine haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) histology would enable single-cell analysis at scale, but training such models has relied on manual pathologist annotations, which are slow, expensive and unreliable for many cell types. We instead supervise morphology with molecules. Imaging-based spatial transcriptomics profiles individual cells in situ on a section that can afterwards be stained with H&E, so that molecular identity and morphology are observed for the same physical cell. We assembled 81 such paired Xenium sections spanning 16 organs, derived per-cell labels by clustering, marker-gene annotation, organ-wise human review and quality control, and mapped them onto the cell types commonly reported in each organ. This yielded 15.4 million cells, each with a paired H&E image patch and one of 23 cell types, on which we trained CytoFormer, a cell foundation model with a multi-task, per-organ classification head. On spatially held-out tissue CytoFormer reached an accuracy of 0.85 and a macro-F1 of 0.78 across all 16 organs, and its predictions reproduced the tissue architecture of an entire held-out section. The representation also transfers: with the encoder frozen, a linear head on CytoFormer features performed better than six pathology foundation models on four expert-annotated benchmarks, including on organs and cell types that were not part of pretraining. Finally, in an interactive active-learning setting, CytoFormer's embeddings are markedly more label-efficient than existing pathology foundation models, detecting normal epithelium amid look-alike tumour with an F1 of 0.82 from only a few annotations and leading the strongest baseline by 0.13 in F1. CytoFormer turns paired H&E and spatial transcriptomics into a reusable, label-efficient representation for cell-level analysis of routine histology.

ultimate.title: AI Predicts Cellular RNA and Proteins From Routine Hospital Slides
ultimate.snippet:
A new artificial intelligence framework successfully reconstructs thousands of hidden cellular molecular profiles directly from routine hospital microscope slides. By analyzing standard tissue sections stained with the pink and purple dyes common in pathology labs, the model predicts both RNA transcript activity and protein distributions at single-cell resolution. Researchers developed the system to unlock molecular insights from massive archives of historical patient samples without requiring expensive, specialized spatial assays.
## Bridging RNA and Protein Data Across Unpaired Tissues
Obtaining detailed maps of gene expression and protein markers across a tissue sample usually demands technically demanding techniques like in situ spatial transcriptomics or multiplex immunofluorescence. Because these advanced assays are costly, laboratories rarely perform both RNA and protein measurements on the exact same tissue section. The research team behind the new model, [published on the arXiv preprint server](http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24104v1), sought to overcome this hurdle by creating a unified system called SCOPE, which stands for Single-Cell Omics Prediction via RNA-protein prior Enhancement.
Led by computer scientists and bioinformaticians from Harvard Medical School, Stanford University, and the Beijing University of Civil Engineering and Architecture, the authors designed their approach around biological connections. Although RNA molecules and proteins represent distinct molecular types, the genes that encode them share a natural biological link. The framework exploits this correspondence to allow supervision from either RNA data or protein data to strengthen a shared gene-level representation.
